passage:
Mentor's note: Mohit, 25, junior architect
In Tuesday's review, a client said, "This looks like a child did it." Mohit went white. Afterwards he asked me for ten minutes. He said the phrase was exactly what his father used to say about his drawings, and it had hit him as if he were twelve again.
He didn't pretend it was nothing. He cried a little, then wrote down what he remembered in his notebook while I sat nearby. He said this has been coming back a lot, so he has booked a session with a counsellor through the office scheme.
I told him I respected how he handled it. Next: I'll share client feedback with him in writing first, then we'll discuss it.
— Sudha

qa.q: What did the client say about the work?
qa.a: "This looks like a child did it."

qa.q: Why did the client's words hit Mohit so hard?
qa.a: It was exactly what his father used to say about his drawings, so an old hurt came rushing back as if he were twelve again.

qa.q: Which of Mohit's choices helped the old hurt settle?
qa.a: Instead of pushing it down, he talked to Sudha, cried, wrote it down, and booked a counsellor because the feeling keeps coming back.

qa.q: How might Sudha's respect affect Mohit?
qa.a: Hearing that his mentor respected how he handled it may help Mohit feel less ashamed of crying at work, and more willing to keep facing it.

grounding: A mentor's note shows a young architect meeting an old hurt by talking, crying and writing, and booking a counsellor as it keeps recurring.

passage:
Thursday, 10:40 pm
The old hurt came back today, out of nowhere. Someone posted our Class 8 photo in the school group, and there I was in the corner, the year everyone called me "the smell" and nobody sat with me at lunch.
My usual trick is to shut the laptop and scrub the whole kitchen. Tonight I didn't. I sat on the floor and cried properly about it for the first time, I think, ever.
Then I called Maria. She didn't say "That was ages ago." She said, "That sounds so lonely." I cried again, but lighter.
If it keeps coming back like this, I'll ask about the counselling service at work. For now: writing, water, sleep.
— Dilnaz

qa.q: What was posted in the school group?
qa.a: The Class 8 photo.

qa.q: Why did Dilnaz cry 'lighter' after talking to Maria?
qa.a: Maria named the loneliness instead of brushing it off, so Dilnaz felt understood and some of the old weight lifted.

qa.q: What choice did Dilnaz make instead of the usual trick?
qa.a: Rather than shutting the laptop and scrubbing the kitchen, Dilnaz let the tears come, called a trusted friend and wrote it down, with counselling as the next step if it keeps returning.

qa.q: What might Maria have felt hearing about the Class 8 year?
qa.a: Maria was probably sad for the younger Dilnaz and glad to be trusted with it 🤍

grounding: A young adult's diary shows an old school hurt met with tears, a call to a trusted friend and writing, with counselling in mind if it persists.

passage: After school in the kasba near Hoshangabad, Vishal, twenty-four, sat alone in the empty staffroom, hands shaking. In class, a boy had frozen at the blackboard and another had jeered, "Useless, just like his father." Vishal had stopped it at once. But the words had hit him too: his own father used to say them. He had thought that was long behind him. His first urge was to shove it down and mark copies. Instead he opened his diary and wrote exactly what he felt, even the angry part. That evening he told his wife, Usha, on the terrace. His voice cracked, and he cried, and she held his hand. "If this keeps coming back and weighs on you," she said, "let's find a counsellor together." Vishal nodded. The next morning, he took the jeering student aside, and then the frozen one.

qa.q: What did the student jeer at the boy at the blackboard?
qa.a: "Useless, just like his father."

qa.q: Why did the jeer hit Vishal so hard?
qa.a: It echoed words his own father used to say to him, bringing back an old hurt he thought was long behind him.

qa.q: What did Vishal choose instead of shoving the feeling down?
qa.a: He wrote exactly what he felt in his diary and later told Usha, letting himself cry, and they agreed to find a counsellor if it kept weighing on him.

qa.q: How might Usha have felt listening to Vishal on the terrace?
qa.a: She seemed caring and steady, holding his hand and offering to look for a counsellor together.

grounding: A young teacher lets an old hurt be spoken by writing and talking to his wife instead of pushing it down, with a counsellor as a possible ally.

passage: At his cousin's wedding in Seville, Alejandro, twenty-six, watched the bride dance with her father, and something old cracked open. His own father had left when he was ten and never came to his graduation. He'd told himself for years that it didn't matter. Now his throat locked and he walked out to the car park. His first instinct was to go back in, smile, and have another drink. Instead he called Zanele, his closest friend from university. "It's stupid," he said. "It was sixteen years ago." "It's not stupid," Zanele said. "Tell me." He talked for twenty minutes and cried twice. Afterward he felt emptied, but lighter. Over the next month the feeling kept coming back at odd moments, so he booked an appointment with a counsellor at the clinic near work. "Good," Zanele texted. "I'm proud of you."

qa.q: How old was Alejandro when his father left?
qa.a: He was ten.

qa.q: Why did Alejandro say "It's stupid" on the phone?
qa.a: Part of him still felt he shouldn't be hurting after sixteen years, as if the old pain didn't deserve attention.

qa.q: Which choices did Alejandro make instead of shoving the feeling down?
qa.a: He called a trusted friend and let himself talk and cry, and when the feeling kept returning, he booked a counsellor.

qa.q: How might Zanele feel hearing Alejandro finally talk about his father?
qa.a: Zanele seemed warm and glad he reached out, and proud of him for booking the counsellor.

grounding: A young man lets an old hurt be spoken with a trusted friend instead of pushing it down, then seeks a counsellor when it persists.
